# Simultaneous facet-contact rigidity for low-efficiency simplex profiles

This is an exact finite geometric restriction on a prescribed cap profile.
It does not assert existence of a Gamma-paying selected circuit in every
mixed family. Its new information is a common anchored affine-contact
relation for all active facets at each unpayable high-profile vertex.

## 1. Compatible common-normal simplex fibers

Let P be a finite integer base of an actual convex mixed family, and let
d>=1. Fix affine barycentric coordinate functions lambda_0,...,lambda_d
on the continuous space, with sum lambda_i=1. Suppose its full-dimensional
fibers are

    K_z={x:lambda_i(x)>=b_i(z), i=0,...,d},
    r_z=1-sum_i b_i(z)>0.                          (1)

All fibers are simplexes with the same oriented facet normals. Their
centers may be nonaffine and their volumes may vary. Convex compatibility
implies the sampled Jensen inequalities

    b_i(p)<=sum_r t_r b_i(z_r)
    whenever p=sum_r t_r z_r, t_r>=0, sum_r t_r=1. (2)

Indeed the actual midpoint/convex combination of the endpoint fibers is
contained in the p-fiber, and taking the minimum of lambda_i gives (2).
No stronger unproved sampled log-concavity statement is used.

Let v_j(z) be the vertex opposite facet j:

    lambda_i(v_j(z))=b_i(z) for i!=j,
    lambda_j(v_j(z))=1-sum_(i!=j)b_i(z).

Let F_i(z) be facet i and form the finite polytope

    B_i=conv union_(z in P)({z} times F_i(z)).      (3)

This is the convex hull of the actual boundary bundle with fixed outward
unit normal n_i. It is not the convex hull of the whole mixed measure.
The vertex (z,v_j(z)) belongs to B_i whenever i!=j.

## 2. Exact equivalence of failure of exposure and common support equality

Fix a base p and a vertex type j. The following are equivalent:

(a) (p,v_j(p)) is not a vertex of B_i for some i!=j.
(b) It is not a vertex of B_i for every i!=j.
(c) There are other bases z_r!=p and positive weights t_r with sum1 such
    that

    p=sum_r t_r z_r,
    b_l(p)=sum_r t_r b_l(z_r) for EVERY l!=j.       (4)

Thus either this vertex is exposed in every incident fixed-normal bundle,
or all its d active support offsets share one nontrivial anchored Jensen
equality. In a finite polytope, being a vertex is equivalent to being the
unique maximizer of an affine functional, so 'exposed' here is literal.

Proof of (a)=> (c). Express (p,v_j(p)) as a convex combination of other
vertices of B_i. These are actual lifted fiber vertices (z_r,x_r). For
each l!=j, use (2) and the lower fiber bound to obtain

    b_l(p)=lambda_l(v_j(p))
          =sum_r t_r lambda_l(x_r)
          >=sum_r t_r b_l(z_r)>=b_l(p).

All inequalities are equalities. Every positive term therefore satisfies
lambda_l(x_r)=b_l(z_r) for all l!=j, forcing x_r=v_j(z_r). The representation
thus has a single vertex type and gives (4). Any term with base p is the
original lifted vertex itself and can be removed by renormalizing the
remaining weights; a nontrivial representation has remaining mass.

Conversely (4) determines all barycentric coordinates of the average and
therefore gives

    (p,v_j(p))=sum_r t_r(z_r,v_j(z_r)).

Every term belongs to every B_i with i!=j. This proves (c)=>(b), and (b)
immediately implies (a).

When the support-offset functions are considered on the actual continuous
projection, they are convex: b_i(z)=min_(x in C_z)lambda_i(x). Equation (4)
then means each of these d functions is affine on the SAME convex hull of
the selected bases. This last statement also follows elementarily. If
f(p)=sum t_r f(z_r) with all t_r>0, take any y=sum s_r z_r and choose
small epsilon>0 with t_r-epsilon s_r>=0. Writing
p=epsilon y+(1-epsilon)z and applying convexity twice forces
f(y)=sum s_r f(z_r). Thus the affine interpolation holds everywhere on
that hull, with no differentiability or supporting-gradient assumption.

## 3. A strict high-profile exposed vertex gives an actual paying hinge

Let H_1,...,H_N be a finite list of actual closed ambient halfspaces,
theta_l>=0 with sum theta_l=1, and

    W=sum_l theta_l 1_Hl.

For a point X define its strict captured weight by

    W_strict(X)=sum_(l:X lies strictly inside H_l)theta_l.       (5)

This treats boundary mass safely: caps whose boundary contains X are not
counted in (5), although their actual contributions are nonnegative.

Suppose X=(p,v_j(p)) is exposed in B_i for some i!=j. Let A be an affine
functional uniquely maximized there, with maximum h. For sufficiently
small delta>0 the potential

    Phi(n,z,x)=psi(n)[A(z,x)-h+delta]_+             (6)

is supported, on the actual normal bundle, in an arbitrarily small
neighborhood of X inside {p} times F_i(p). Here psi is continuous and
nonnegative on the unit-normal sphere, equals1 at n_i and0 at the other
finitely many distinct facet normals. Such psi can be given by a product
of squared distances from those other normals, normalized at n_i.

To justify the localization, all other vertices of the finite polytope
B_i have a strictly smaller A value. Hence the positive hinge is supported
near its unique maximizing vertex and, for a sufficiently small delta,
on no other base's facet. Its integral is strictly positive: each
(d-1)-dimensional simplex facet has a positive-measure corner neighborhood
at each of its vertices. For d=1 this is the positive counting mass of
that endpoint. The potential is nonnegative, continuous and physically
convex for each fixed normal; its denominator is finite.

Every strictly positive cap margin at X remains positive in a small
neighborhood. Thus throughout the support of (6), W>=W_strict(X), and

    integral Phi W d eta / integral Phi d eta >=W_strict(X).   (7)

If no cap boundary passes through X, all cap signs remain fixed and the
ratio equals W(X) exactly. The statement uses actual point exposure,
not the false assertion that a whole exposed facet permits concentration
at an arbitrary point of its relative interior.

## 4. The resulting rigidity condition

Let E(W) be the supremum of the efficiency over all nonnegative continuous
normal-dependent physically convex potentials. Combining Sections2--3
proves:

**Rigidity lemma.** If E(W)<=c, then every lifted fiber vertex X with
W_strict(X)>c has a nontrivial anchored representation (4), with simultaneous
affine contact of all d active support offsets.

Equivalently, if just one high-weight vertex lacks this common contact
relation, an explicit admissible hinge already disproves E(W)<=c.
Neither genuine criticality nor global deepestness is needed for this
geometric implication. When applied to a genuine critical circuit, those
assumptions remain available as additional restrictions on (4), rather
than being silently inferred from it.

One convenient sufficient condition for payment is that for a high-weight
vertex, at least one active b_l has a strict Jensen inequality at p in
EVERY nontrivial representation by other bases. More generally, individual
active offsets may have nontrivial affine relations while their common
contact set is trivial; the joint condition in (4) retains that distinction.

## 5. Exact calibration and limitation

In the actual R4 perturbation b_i(z)=e ell_i(z)^2, equality for either
active offset forces its ell_i values to be constant on all representation
bases. At a planar simplex vertex the two active ell_i are linearly
independent, so simultaneous equality forces all bases to equal p. Thus
every lifted fiber vertex is exposed in every incident bundle. The fiber
at (1,1) has strict profile weight2/3; it necessarily admits a paying
hinge. The previous source gives that hinge explicitly, not just via a
separation theorem.

This also explains why a finite strict efficiency gap at the undeformed
product does not automatically persist under small facet-offset changes:
new exposed vertices can appear in the normal bundle, and the optimizing
convex potentials have no uniform slope bound.

The condition is deliberately pointwise. Even for an ordinary triangle
with the canonical three centroid caps, the profile has boundary essential
supremum2/3, while its full convex-potential optimum is4/9. High values on
the interior of an exposed EDGE cannot be isolated by a convex hinge.
A proposed 1/2 bound obtained from opposite rays therefore needs actual
point exposure, not merely exposed fixed-normal facets. No general
selected-circuit Gamma theorem is proved here.

## 6. A finite sufficient certificate for favorable circuit selection

The rigidity lemma gives a new exact finite test in the selected-circuit
problem. Fix a finite regular critical cap menu at a source and use its
scale-invariant response vectors b_l=S_l u_l. Let

    T={theta>=0:sum theta=1, sum theta_l b_l=0},

as in `candidate b1ef83513bdb0bcf`.
Assume T is nonempty. Let X range over all actual lifted fiber vertices
which lack the common contact relation (4), and put

    h_X,l=1 if X is strictly inside H_l, and 0 otherwise.

Then the achievable selected-circuit efficiency has the proved lower bound

    E_N >= max_X max_(theta in T) sum_l h_X,l theta_l.           (8)

Indeed choose a maximizing finite-menu response weight vector, then apply
the exposed-point hinge construction. The inner maximum is an ordinary
finite linear program and is attained, with a maximizer supported on at
most d+1 caps. Its exact dual is

    inf_(v in R^d) max_l [h_X,l-v dot b_l].                     (9)

Thus a value at least Gamma_d in (8) is a concrete, finite sufficient
certificate, using actual critical caps and actual common-facet contact
geometry. No global lower bound for (8) is asserted. Empty X lists or
values below Gamma merely mean this particular test gives no certificate;
interior-facet potentials may still pay.

For the R4 product's bad diagonal circuit this exposed-vertex test sees
only weight1/3 at its extreme bundles. For the quadratic perturbation,
the new exposed vertex at (1,1) gives2/3 for the same diagonal weights.
For the favorable symmetry-selected product orbit, an exposed base fiber
is fully captured by every row, so (8) has value1. These are exact
geometric distinctions, not a numerical optimization heuristic.

## 7. A complementary sufficient condition: exact whole-fiber radial localization

Suppose p is strictly exposed on EVERY sampled lower support graph:
for each i there is an affine function a_i dot(z-p) such that

    b_i(z)>b_i(p)+a_i dot(z-p) for every z!=p.      (10)

This is a separate sufficient condition, not a consequence of the previous
contact lemma. Let y be any interior point of K_p, and let

    r_i=n_i dot(x-y)>0 for x in F_i(p),

its constant radial facet flux. Choose delta_i>0 smaller than all the
finite strict gaps in (10). With the same normal selectors as before,
define

    Phi(n,z,x)=sum_i psi_i(n)(r_i/delta_i)
          [delta_i+b_i(p)+a_i dot(z-p)-lambda_i(x)]_+.         (11)

At normal n_i this equals r_i on the whole facet F_i(p) and zero on
F_i(z) for every z!=p. The other normal selectors vanish there. Thus
on the ACTUAL boundary bundle (11) is exactly the own-fiber radial
velocity n dot(x-y), and zero on every other fiber. It is nonnegative,
continuous, and physically convex for each fixed normal. Its denominator
is d|K_p|.

For any closed cap through (p,y), the continuous cut-plane radial flux
vanishes. Hence its numerator contribution is exactly d times its
ordinary own-fiber cap volume. If its continuous normal is zero, the
through-source cap contains the whole own fiber and the same identity
is d|K_p|. Therefore for an arbitrary normalized finite through-source
profile,

    integral Phi W d eta / integral Phi d eta
       =sum_j theta_j |K_p intersect H_j|/|K_p|.   (12)

In particular this is at least the ordinary depth of y in K_p. If y is
the actual centroid, or any ordinary center whose depth is at least
Gamma_d, it pays Gamma_d. No criticality or circuit balance is needed
for this sufficient result, but the source condition cannot be discarded.
A whole facet is only being localized uniformly; no illicit concentration
at its relative-interior profile maximum occurs.
